articles.headline: Trump and Putin to hold one-on-one meeting at Asia summit
keyFacts: U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a one-on-one meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, a U.S. official confirmed.
The upcoming discussion follows their previous meeting in Alaska in August 2025 regarding the Russia-Ukraine war, which did not result in a ceasefire.
The exact timing of the bilateral meeting remains unclear, though Putin approached Trump to shake hands ahead of a planned trilateral meeting.
body: President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet one-on-one on the sidelines of the Asia -Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, a U.S. official confirmed to the Washington Examiner .

This will be their first meeting since they met in Alaska in August 2025 to discuss the Russia-Ukraine war . Their meeting on U.S. soil did not lead to a meaningful ceasefire in the conflict, despite Trump’s public desire for the war to end.
Trump feted Putin with a red carpet rollout in Alaska and a ride in the presidential limo, even as allies had shunned the Russian leader for his attacks on Ukraine.
The exact timing of Trump and Putin’s meeting is unclear.

At APEC, Putin made a point of approaching Trump, who was chatting with Chinese President Xi Jinping , to shake his hand. It was the first time the three leaders were seen together ahead of their unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , where APEC is being held.

Before the family photo meeting, Xi had made the rare move to meet Trump on the tarmac when he landed in Shenzhen, mirroring Trump’s decision to meet Xi at Joint Base Andrews when he visited in September.
The trilateral meeting has sparked some fears among other world leaders that major decisions could be made without their input.
CHINA’S XI JINPING GREETS TRUMP AT AIRPORT IN RARE MOVE

The United States has led the charge to broker a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and some Europea n allies fear a potential deal could include tough concessions from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Putin’s presence at APEC, along with his high-profile meetings with Xi and Trump, is another global stage for the Russian leader to gain attention despite efforts to isolate his nation due to the war with Ukraine.

articles.headline: Iran ramps up attacks on Gulf countries after U.S. strikes
keyFacts: Bahrain and Kuwait reported intercepting weapons launched by Iran following U.S. strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island.
A crew member was missing and eleven people were injured after an ADNOC oil company ship was struck in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the energy firm.
Saudi Arabia is preparing for its war against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen to continue into 2027, according to Western officials.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Bahrain and Kuwait said Wednesday that they intercepted weapons launched by after the U.S. carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran appears to be stepping up attacks on America's Persian Gulf allies as tension ratchets back up across the region.

- A U.S. official called the Tuesday strikes on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island a defensive response to Iranian forces "targeting U.S. personnel and assets" in the region. The strikes came hours after Iran said it targeted a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain for the third time in less than a week. Those attacks were all intercepted, U.S. authorities said.

- A crew member was missing Wednesday after a ship belonging to the United Arab Emirates' state oil company ADNOC was struck in the Strait of Hormuz, the energy firm said. Eleven people were injured, and search and rescue operations were ongoing, according to ADNOC.
U.S. intelligence chief says Iranian threats inside and outside U.S. have "dramatically increased"
U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Wednesday that Iranian threats inside and outside the U.S. have "dramatically increased."

"We remain committed to detecting, deterring and combatting the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton told members of the House Homeland Security Committee during a hearing. "These threats have dramatically increased."
He emphasized the danger posed by online radicalization, describing how foreign extremist networks can influence individuals already living inside the United States.
"That's not theoretical; it's real," Clayton said.
Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia noted that intelligence about possible plots does not necessarily mean would-be attackers have the capability to carry out the plans.
"A lot of the reporting is largely aspirational," Raia said. "But that does not mean we do not take it seriously."
Saudi Arabia preparing for Yemen war to continue into 2027, Western officials tell Reuters

Saudi Arabia is preparing for its war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen to last well into 2027, the Reuters news agency reported Wednesday, citing two Western officials briefed by the kingdom about its planning.

Fighting in Yemen's grueling civil war between the Houthi rebels and Yemen's Saudi-backed government had largely stopped after a ceasefire was signed in 2022, but reignited over the summer as the war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran sent tension across the Middle East surging.

The exchange of fire between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been more intense than the other fronts in the intertwined Middle Eastern conflicts since U.S.-Iran hostilities eased late in the summer. Thousands of people have been killed and hundreds of thousands displaced in Yemen, and Houthi rockets have killed at least 20 people in Saudi Arabia.

Saudi authorities have acknowledged Houthi targeting of key infrastructure in the kingdom, including airports and oil facilities. The kingdom now expects the campaign to last up to six more months, Reuters said, adding that Saudi officials are hoping to see advances on the ground before re-entering negotiations with the Houthis.
This week, however, has seen Yemeni government-aligned forces pull back from some key territory on the Red Sea coast as the Houthis take more ground.
U.S. military shares images of 2 aircraft carriers together in Middle East
The U.S. military's Central Command shared new images Wednesday of the USS Theodore Roosevelt and USS George Washington aircraft carriers sailing in tandem in the Arabian Sea.

CENTCOM included a photo compilation of the two nuclear-powered carriers in a post on X that offered no information, just a date and the vague location of the carrier in the sea, which is southeast of the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf beyond.

The U.S. military's naval presence in the Gulf of Oman, the Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean is currently greater than the force deployed during Operation Epic Fury, at the peak of U.S. and Iranian hostilities, according to an open source intelligence analysis by the independent Israeli think tank The Institute for National Security Studies.

The U.S. military confirmed Monday that there are now three aircraft carrier strike groups in the region after the recent arrival of the USS Roosevelt. It joined the USS George H.W. Bush and USS Washington, alongside a slew of associated destroyers and other vessels.
The three-carrier presence is expected to be temporary, as carrier strike groups rotate through the region.
Iran denies any link to alleged "terrorist plot" in North Macedonia
Iran on Wednesday rejected as "completely unfounded" an assertion by authorities in North Macedonia that they had uncovered a Tehran-backed assassination plot targeting a person in Greece.
The Iranian Embassy in Greece called the "baseless accusations" part of a "worn-out campaign by the Israeli regime and its propaganda and psychological warfare apparatuses to discredit Iran."
North Macedonia's National Security Agency said Tuesday that it had foiled an alleged plot and dismantled a network linked to Iran in cooperation with Greek intelligence.

Four suspects are in custody and a fifth under house arrest in North Macedonia, the authorities said. One suspect was arrested in Greece and handed over to North Macedonian authorities, Greek officials said, according to the AFP news agency.
Some Greek media, including the ERT state broadcaster and the daily Kathimerini, reported that the target was allegedly an Israeli-born executive of an Israeli company based in Greece.

According to North Macedonia's security agency, the dismantled network included "proxy actors" linked to Iranian national Edris Jahangiri Mavaneh, who was a "collaborator of the Iranian security and intelligence services."

The network, "under the direct instructions of the Iranian national, undertook preparatory logistical activities to carry out a terrorist act/assassination against a person in Greece," the agency said.
CBS/AFP
U.S.-Saudi nuclear agreement "very satisfactory," says U.N. nuclear watchdog agency IAEA

The head of the IAEA, the United Nations nuclear watchdog agency, described on Wednesday a deal that could see the United States help equip Saudi Arabia with a civilian nuclear program as "very satisfactory."
The has drawn questions about the risks of possible nuclear proliferation.

"It's a very satisfactory outcome that we have with this agreement," Grossi told reporters after opening an International Atomic Energy Agency board of governors' meeting, according to the AFP news agency.
The IAEA chief said if and when nuclear power development gets under way in Saudi Arabia, "we will be there."

In his opening statement, Grossi told the board the U.S. and Saudi Arabia had asked the IAEA in October "to take the necessary steps to implement safeguards and verification measures" for their agreement.

Under the deal, the IAEA "will be provided with information about, and access to any sites for conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication and reprocessing" in Saudi Arabia, Grossi said, adding that he welcomed "the open, transparent approach and engagement of both governments with member states and the secretariat on this matter."
Saudi Arabia had also agreed to "additional verification measures on a voluntary basis," Grossi said.
President Trump said after the agreement was signed that moving forward on the deal would be contingent upon Saudi Arabia signing onto the Abraham Accords, formally normalizing relations with Israel.
CBS/AFP
U.S. naval presence in Mideast now greater than during peak of war with Iran, think tank says

The U.S. military's naval presence in the Gulf of Oman, the Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean is currently greater than the force that was deployed during Operation Epic Fury, at the peak of U.S. and Iranian hostilities, according to an open source intelligence analysis by the Institute for National Security Studies, an independent think tank in Israel.

The U.S. military confirmed Monday that there are now three aircraft carrier strike groups in the region after the recent arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt. That carrier joined the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, alongside with a slew of destroyers and other vessels.
The three-carrier presence is expected to be temporary, however, as carrier strike groups rotate through the region.

According to an interactive map published by the INSS, the U.S. has deployed 12 destroyers to the Arabian Sea, one of which appears to be positioned just inside the Gulf of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The map indicates that there are not currently any U.S. warships in the Persian Gulf or the gateway to it, the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran and the U.S. both claim control over.
A senior Iranian military figure said in late October that the regime "will not allow U.S. military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time."

"The U.S. president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf," Iranian armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi was quoted as saying by state TV. "He will take that dream to his grave."

The INSS map does show two U.S destroyers in the Red Sea, where the Iran-backed Houthi rebels have recently expanded their control over Yemen's coastline on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, threatening Saudi Arabia's oil exports.
Iranian protesters criticize regime in rare public demonstration after deadly bus crash

Some demonstrators who gathered in western Iranian town offered rare public criticism of the Islamic Republic regime Tuesday during a protest over the deaths of 13 gas and oil workers in a bus crash, according to eyewitness accounts.
While Iran's tightly controlled media outlets portrayed the gathering in the city of Abdanan as a protest over road safety, eyewitnesses said the demonstration took on an anti-government tone.

Iran's Fars News Agency, which is closely affiliated with the country's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, reported that the protest grew to around 1,000 people, and it acknowledged that slogans chanted by attendees had a "political tone."

"At first, people were mostly angry about the accident, but gradually the slogans became political and against the government," Jamshid, a shopkeeper who witnessed the demonstration, told CBS News over the phone.
He said "security forces eventually dispersed the crowd by force, using tear gas and even shooting warning shots."
State broadcaster IRIB called the gathering "another failure of the counter-revolution plan" and claimed residents had come out to quell the unrest themselves in support of the government.
A resident of Iran's capital Tehran, who asked to remain anonymous due to concerns for his safety, disputed the state broadcaster's account.

"The accident brought people into the streets, but the anger wasn't only about the workers who died," he told CBS News. "People were chanting against the government, even against the new supreme leader, and some were supporting the ."
Saudi coalition says major attack on Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen destroyed "60 legitimate military targets"

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iranian-backed Houthis said Wednesday it launched a major air attack across territory held by the rebels in Yemen. The Houthis said the Saudi strikes killed at least 17 people.

Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi coalition, said the strikes launched Tuesday destroyed "60 legitimate military targets" in Yemen's Houthi-held capital Sanaa, and the provinces of Amran, Saada and Hodeida.

The strikes aimed to weaken the Houthis' missile and drone capabilities by destroying tunnels into mountain warehouses where ballistic missiles are stored, and workshops used to assemble and store drones, al-Maliki said.

Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Houthi-run health ministry, said one strike hit a sponge factory in Hodeida, killing at least 15 people and wounding 13 others. Another strike in the district of Kitaf in Saada killed at least two people and wounded four others. In Sanaa, at least nine people were wounded in a strike that hit a shoe factory, al-Asbahi said.
CBS/AP
Bahrain, Kuwait say they fended off strikes by Iran

Bahrain and Kuwait claimed Wednesday that they repelled air attacks launched against them, as Gulf nations face retaliatory bombardment following U.S. strikes on an Iranian island.The Iranian army said Wednesday its drones "targeted Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms belonging to the terrorist U.S. military at Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait," in a statement carried by state television IRIB.
Kuwait's military said Wednesday its air defenses were "responding to hostile drone threats" and urged the public to follow security and safety advice.

The foreign ministry said in a statement posted on social media that "the continuation of these attacks constitutes a dangerous escalation that threatens the region's security and stability and undermines diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalation."
Meanwhile, Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted attacks early Wednesday, a day after Tehran's Revolutionary Guard said it struck a base used by the U.S.
Iran's official IRNA news agency cited a regional official as saying the United States had hit Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz but did not cause serious damage.
CBS/AFP
Iraq resumes pumping oil through pipeline to Turkey in order to avoid Strait of Hormuz

Iraq has resumed pumping oil to Turkey through a pipeline at an initial capacity of 120,000 barrels a day, Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair al-Abadi said Tuesday in comments carried by state media. The export capacity will be gradually increased to reach 500,000 barrels a day, he said.

The capacity is fairly small compared to other pipelines in the region. The Saudi East-West pipeline, which crosses from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea in order to avoid the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, has a capacity of 7 million barrels per day.
In August, Iraq and Turkey signed a deal to increase oil exports through a pipeline to the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
Iraq is moving to strengthen the resilience of its oil export infrastructure following the U.S.-Iran war's disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iraq-Turkey pipeline has been largely idle since 2023 following legal and commercial disputes.
CBS/AP
One crew member missing after ship struck in Strait of Hormuz, UAE state oil firm says
The United Arab Emirates' oil firm ADNOC said Wednesday that a crew member was missing after one of its ships was struck the night before in the Strait of Hormuz.

"All other crew members have been safely evacuated from the vessel. Eleven sustained injuries and where required are receiving medical care," ADNOC said, adding that search and rescue operations were continuing.

Monitoring agencies report ships being attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on a near-daily basis. Iran claims it carried out some of the attacks on ships it considers transiting through the waterway without its permission.
The U.S. military has also previously said it struck and halted ships it deems to be violating its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
CBS/AFP
U.S. announces "self-defense" strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island
The U.S. launched precision strikes on an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps missile site on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a U.S. military official.
The official said the strike was launched "in self-defense."

"The strike was in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets," the official said. "U.S. Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region."
While the official did not specifically mention the IRGC aggression, the strikes came hours after Iran targeted a U.S. radar site in Bahrain. The s

This was the third attempted strike by Iran on a U.S. military installation in the last five days. All of them were intercepted, U.S. officials said.trikes were successfully intercepted, according to U.S. Central Command.

Iran had earlier said the U.S. attacked Qeshm Island, but they "caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas," according to Ahmad Nafisi, deputy provincial governor of the southern province of Hormozgan, quoted by the official IRNA news agency.

articles.headline: Recent service outages not state-sponsored attacks, DNI Jay Clayton testifies
keyFacts: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified that recent U.S. service outages stem from routine technical issues rather than coordinated foreign attacks.
Clayton warned lawmakers that rapid advancements in artificial intelligence are escalating the speed and sophistication of future cyber threats.
Clayton also highlighted increased Iranian plotting and urged Congress to renew Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act.
body: Recent service outages across U.S. systems stem from routine technical and maintenance issues – not a coordinated foreign cyberattack, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified Wednesday, even as he warned lawmakers that "superintelligence" is rapidly escalating the speed and sophistication of future cyber threats.

"Based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, " Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee's "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11" hearing. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

Clayton acknowledged public concern over the timing of the recent outages, telling the panel that the American people are right to ask questions, but intelligence reviews point away from foreign interference.

"We have no indication that these events are related," Clayton said in response to persistent questioning from Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y. "But let me answer something that the American people should know, which is the speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially, which means legacy systems that were old six months ago or a year are a lot older."
The intelligence community remains on alert and continues to monitor for any malicious cyber activity targeting U.S. networks or law enforcement partners, Clayton said in his opening statement.

"After doing a great deal of due diligence inside the government with the private sector, with people in the private sector whose job is cybersecurity, we have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton reiterated in the question and answer session of the hearing. "We also have no indication that they're a result of a state-sponsored malign actor."

Beyond the immediate outages, the intelligence chief warned lawmakers that rapid advancements in artificial intelligence – also referred to as "superintelligence" – are fundamentally altering the digital battlefield and raising the stakes for homeland defense.

"Let me note that superintelligence is reshaping the cybersecurity landscape, " Clayton said. "It is sharply increasing speed, scale, and sophistication of offensive and defensive cyber operations. And it's not just cyber. This goes to national security. It goes to the battlefield and it goes to commerce. Superintelligence is changing the way we do business, the way we fight wars and the way we combat terrorism every day."

During his opening remarks, Clayton outlined a broader heightened threat environment 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks. While declining to discuss classified intelligence in an open setting, he noted that full briefings have been provided to the Gang of Eight and congressional intelligence committees.
Among the primary threats highlighted in his testimony:

- Iranian plotting: Clayton said threats from Iran – both inside the United States and targeting Americans abroad – have "substantially increased," underscoring a commitment to detecting and deterring lethal plots.

- Terrorism: While post-9/11 counterterrorism efforts have degraded the capabilities of major groups, Clayton warned of persistent threats from individuals inspired by ISIS and al-Qaeda, as well as networks exploited by adversarial nations.

Surveillance authorities: Clayton urged Congress not to let Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) expire, calling it the "single most indispensable tool" for early warnings on foreign threats to the homeland and U.S. troops.
"No other program can replicate the speed and effectiveness of FISA 702," Clayton said. "Letting it expire would simply be a mistake."

articles.headline: MongoDB snaps up Firebolt to bring transactions and analytics under one roof
keyFacts: MongoDB acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt to combine transactional and analytical workloads onto a single platform.
MongoDB stated that integrating Firebolt's engine will provide a high-performance analytics engine alongside operational data without requiring data pipelines.
MongoDB announced that customers will gain access to the integrated features in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will keep their service.
body: MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform.

The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications.
It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability.

Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020 , then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency.
Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price.
But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users?

In a blog post , the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure."
The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support.
MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together.

MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part.

Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem , promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level.

SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system.
Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analyzing it.

MongoDB promises real-time analytics without a customer-managed pipeline. Whether that also means avoiding separate copies of the data is less clear. Automatic synchronization doesn't explain how the information is stored or moved underneath. The Register has asked MongoDB to clarify the architecture.

MongoDB has been here before. In 2022, it unveiled columnstore indexing designed to help developers build analytical queries into their applications. The idea was to accelerate those queries without changing the document structure or moving data to another system.
Firebolt gives MongoDB another tool for a familiar job: making analytics feel at home beside its operational database. Whether the plumbing lives up to the pitch remains to be seen. ®

articles.headline: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
keyFacts: Ukrainian forces have been fighting Russian troops inside an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region for seven months.
The pipeline offers relative safety from drones that saturate the skies and prevent troops from advancing above ground.
The BBC reported on the subterranean battle from near Kupyansk after entering the pipeline with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.
body: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.

With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.

articles.headline: 32 Spoiler-Free Tips As You Hop Into Grand Theft Auto 6
keyFacts: Grand Theft Auto 6 features a deep and complex world with various gameplay mechanics like eating, drinking, and petting animals to boost character stats.
Players can utilize tools like the Scooter Bros app, focus mode, and clothing store management to navigate the game world and evade the police.
Reviewers recommend that players avoid spoilers, take their time exploring the map, and investigate random events to fully experience the game.
body: Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here. The long wait was totally worth it. It is one of the best games I’ve played in many years and easily the best Grand Theft Auto game ever made. It is also a big, complicated, and deep game, with so much to do and see.
So, to help you out, here’s a bunch of tips for players hopping into GTA 6 this week. Don’t worry, no spoilers are included below.
Try To Avoid Spoilers Or Looking Up Secrets

Without spoiling anything, there are some incredibly big surprises and really memorable moments buried in this game. I highly recommend that people avoid watching too many videos about GTA 6 ahead of playing it to avoid ruining one particular late-game moment that might be one of my favorite video game surprises in years.
Drink And Eat Before Heading Out

Before you rush out the door to do some missions or rob a liquor store, take a moment to grab a bite and a drink. These items will buff your health, stamina, and focus meter, letting you take more damage, run longer, and slow down time more during combat.
You Can Eat And Drink While Driving Or Shooting

And hey, don’t assume that just because you’re drinking a soda or eating a hot dog, you have to stop moving or shooting. In GTA 6, you can move, shoot, run, hold hands, and even drive while holding and eating food. Finally, you can crack a cold one while shooting a rifle.
Pet Dogs And Cats To Buff Focus

Around the map, you’ll encounter dogs and cats. If you hold the left trigger, you can zoom in on them and then praise and pet them. And you should do this, not just because dogs and cats are great, but also because it buffs your focus and rewards you with some good behavior points toward your criminal profile.
Always Keep A Few Outfits In The Trunk
In GTA 6, you can store guns and clothes in your personal car’s trunk. And you should do this, as changing clothes is a great and fast way to lose the attention of the police.
Manage Outfits While Out And About Via Clothing Stores

You can manage your clothing, create new custom outfits, and store clothes in your trunk at any clothing store with a changing room, so don’t feel like you have to head back home to change your outfits around or remove stuff from your trunk. Just find a store.
Rename Custom Outfits To Make Dress-Up Easier

Also, Rockstar lets you rename your custom outfits using a list of pre-existing words, like clubbing, hunting, or everyday. I recommend doing that to make it easier at a glance to see what everything stored in your trunk actually is without having to put it on and check.
Shop As A Couple

When you go out shopping for clothesâand you will likely do that because dressing up is so much fun in this gameâbring both Jason and Lucia. This will let you buy clothing for both of them, try on new items as either character, and modify their current attire. And bonus: Buying clothing for your partner gets you some extra romance points.
If You Hear Shouting Or Sirens, Use Focus To Find The Source And Go Investigate

The world of Leonida is packed with random events and moments that you can encounter while just walking around. These can be as simple as a drug deal going bad, or as complex as someone who needs help finding their missing spouse after a night partying. Often these events will be signaled to the player via shouting or other loud noises. If you hear something like that, click the left and right sticks to activate focus mode and find the source of the commotion, and then go investigate it.
Your Trunk Closes Automatically

I spent many hours making sure to close it first, then realized it closed when you drive away. You can also hold left on the D-pad to access your car’s features, including the ability to turn off headlights and close (or open) the trunk.
Regularly Check Your Phoneâs Reminders

This section of Jason and Lucia’s phone will update as you play and will remind you to call certain characters or reply to texts. This can often reveal new story moments and dialogue between Lucia and Jason and their various friends and criminal cohorts.
Do Underwater Treasure Hunts For Easy Early Money

Very early into GTA 6, you unlock the ability to explore underwater shipwrecks and find valuable loot. And you should do some of these in the early hours of GTA 6 to earn some easy cash. Plus, it’s just fun to explore the ocean.
Use The Scooter Bros App

On Jason and Lucia’s phones, you’ll find an app called Scooter Bros. This lets you manage your owned vehicles, spawn them near you, and even repair them. However, this isn’t free and early on money will be tight, so be careful how often you rely on this convenient app. It can also get vehicles out of police impound lots, but that ain’t cheap.
And When You Can Afford It, Upgrade To Scooter Bros Premium

It costs $12,500 to upgrade to the premium version of the Scooter Bros service, which, for many hours in the game, is going to be more than you can spare. But once you feel comfortable spending that much, I recommend it. It gives you three free uses of the app every in-game day, which saves money in the long run. Plus, the app is upgraded and says you’re premium, and that’s nice.
Buy Garages When You Can To Store More Vehicles

Eventually, GTA 6 will let you buy garages around the map. These aren’t very useful while driving about, but they do give you more slots to store cars and motorcycles as you build up Jason and Lucia’s fleet of personal vehicles. Try to buy some when you can so you can have a wide array of customized bikes, cars, and trucks at your disposal.
You Can Use Your Turn Signals

You don’t have to, but if you want to do so, just tap left or right to signal to other drivers which way you are turning. In my testing, NPC drivers did seem to react to these signals. One more silly detail in GTA 6.Â
Tag Enemies To Keep Track Of Them

Jason and Lucia can both tag enemies while aiming at them with weapons or using binoculars. This will let you keep track of them and make sneaking around compounds much easier. Oh, and don’t forget to use focus to see enemies making noise and moving around, too.
Use Binoculars To Study From A Distance
Binocs can also be used to study the many, many animals in GTA 6 from a safe distance.
Use Focus To Spot Alarmed Doors And Guards

When sneaking into a place to rob it, use focus to spot which doors are connected to the alarm system quickly. These doors will glow red. Avoid kicking these doors in and work around them or lockpick them once you have that tool.
Buy Zombix At Most Convenience Stores

Zombix is the in-game medicine that you can pop during combat to heal up. You can find it in the world for free. But if you need some, you can also buy it at stores. Just talk to the clerk to buy some, as it’s often not stocked in the store like food and drinks.
Repair Cars At Gas Stations

Refueling cars is the main purpose of gas stations, but don’t forget you can also repair your car or motorcycle for a small fee at any gas pump, too. This is often cheaper than using the Scooter Bros app.
Hold Down To Mark Nearby Locations

In GTA 6, you can hold down on the D-pad to slow down time and see nearby points of interest, missions, and other locations worth checking out. You can also mark any of these spots, and then the game will give you directions via the GPS. It’s faster than opening the map and useful for finding nearby gas stations if you’re running low on fuel.
Avoid Cars With Advanced Trackers Until Later In The Game

If you steal a car and you spot a red tracking icon in the bottom left, near the engine and gas icons, you should probably get out quickly. That red icon indicates the car is fitted with an advanced tracker, and police will be able to find you on the map if you drive slowly for too long. You’ll want to avoid these cars until much later in the game when you get the ability to remove these trackers for a high cost. Use the Waink app on your phone by holding up on the D-pad to quickly scan cars and check for trackers.
Defuse Situations To Avoid Violence And The Police

In GTA 6, cops won’t always pull their guns out and try to arrest or shoot you. Instead, a one-star wanted level can be erased if you just talk to the cop and defuse the situation. Hold the left trigger to focus on the cop (make sure you don’t have a gun out), and you’ll see the option to defuse or provoke the cop. This works on any NPC and might let you avoid violence. Some people will still attack or harass regardless of whether you try to stay calm and defuse the situation, though.
If You Feel Vibration While On Foot, There Might Be Something To Scan

While exploring the map, if you feel a sudden and intense vibration pulsing in your controller, stop and look around with the Waink app. There’s likely some art or something else worth scanning nearby.
Always Throw Away Your Garbage
Don’t be a litterbug. Giving a hoot boosts your focus and gives you some good behavior points.
Most Clothing Stores And Hair Salons Have Exclusive Items

While you’ll be able to find similar items and hairstyles at all stores and barber shops, most of these places also have exclusive options available only at that spot. So exploreÂ and see what you can find.
You Can Shave Your Beard And Head In Your Safehouse Bathroom

If you just want a quick and simple trim, you can always look at your mirror in your safehouse bathroom and cut your hair down. You can’t change the style beyond that, though. I guess only the barbers and stylists in Vice City have the magic power to make hair grow back instantly.
Be Careful Entering The Water

Leonida is Rockstar’s digital recreation of Florida. And as someone who grew up in Florida, I was raised to always assume a gator is in every body of water. That’s a good rule of thumb when playing GTA 6, too.
Use RydeMe To âFast Travelâ Long Distances

While I encourage everyone to take their time (see next tip), if you really want to get somewhere fast, just use the RydeMe app to call a driver, and then once you’re in the car, hold the left trigger to focus on the driver and get the option to fast travel to your destination for $100.
Go Slow, Baby

Listen, how long have you already waited to play this game? Trust me, it’s worth slowing down and taking it all in. There’s so much to see, do, and discover out there, and most of it will pass you by if you speedrun the game.

articles.headline: Sam Altman warns against a future where AI, not humans, calls the shots
keyFacts: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated at a summit that humans must remain in control of the future rather than handing decision-making authority over to artificial intelligence.
Altman and OpenAI President Greg Brockman discussed challenges regarding artificial intelligence alignment, safety, and security as models become increasingly more powerful and capable.
Brockman noted that advancing artificial intelligence capabilities will require new monitoring approaches because traditional methods like chain-of-thought tracking may become degraded.
body: OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about whether there will be a gradual handover to AI — meaning AI will eventually become the decision-making authority across every major industry and institution.

“One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And I — we both — agree that that’s a terrible idea,” said Altman, who was sharing the stage with OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman.

The handoff theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI. As existing AI technology builds newer, smarter generations, those will eventually become a superintelligence that humans can no longer control, the belief goes.

Altman explained that he and Brockman only disagree over how to best accomplish the goal of keeping humans in control, or what sort of challenges we should expect to face along the way. However, Altman characterized this as more of a debate between two people who share the same larger views.

“The question of how to actually prevent [handover] from happening — how to actually ensure that we will, given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do — that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way, and we don’t have this either accidental or intentional handover — I think we can both agree on that,” Altman said.
Brockman added that, as the models improve, there’s an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, and security, which may require changes in how things are currently done.
“Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new…technology,” he said.

Today, AI researchers monitor the model’s chain of thought, where the AI writes out what it’s thinking as it works through problems and performs tasks. But in Brockman’s view, that may not always be the best way to monitor more advanced AI that’s being built now.

“As the models have gotten more capable, they can do more within just the forward path without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring,” Brockman said. “We’re going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about, as the capabilities get to a certain point, chain-of-thought monitorability is degraded,” he continued, adding that all the problems were technical ones to be solved.

OpenAI had committed to increased chain-of-thought monitoring after the incident where an OpenAI model escaped containment and hacked into the AI model repository Hugging Face. In today’s interview, Brockman noted that the company told 25% of its production engineers to stop building things and work on securing the AI technology after the hack.
But despite the high-profile breach, he argued that forward progress was still critical to fight bad actors.

“I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities of models in the world, and you see cyber models that are coming from that are now…in the hands of threat actors everywhere, that I think that it’s really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend,” he said.

articles.headline: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
keyFacts: United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that Sunday's Vulcan rocket failure was caused by an inadequate fuel supply to the engines.
Preliminary data indicates low booster thrust resulted from the vehicle's fuel delivery rather than the performance of the BE-4 engines.
The findings clear Blue Origin's BE-4 engines and allow the company to proceed toward a potential New Glenn return-to-flight in January.
body: United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply.

“ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the company said in a statement. “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.”

The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket’s failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle’s main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin.
This represents an important revelation from ULA and will provide some major relief to different parts of the US aerospace community, particularly Blue Origin and NASA.
Big for Blue

That’s because the BE-4 engine is also the bedrock of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket. This powerful rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that was later attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.

After this anomaly, Blue Origin retrofitted the main oxygen valve, including for Vulcan missions. Now it’s clear that this retrofit was not implicated in the Vulcan accident. With the preliminary Vulcan investigation having largely exonerated the BE-4 engine, Blue Origin can press ahead with its return-to-flight mission with New Glenn, which could occur as soon as January.

“Following the Vulcan anomaly, Blue Origin immediately worked alongside ULA to review flight data and support the investigation,” Blue Origin said in a statement Wednesday. “Together, we identified that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines. ULA is a valued partner, and we look forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.”

articles.headline: 74% of shoppers trust AI agents for buying advice – but checkout is another story
keyFacts: Salesforce research shows 74 percent of holiday shoppers trust recommendations from AI agents, though most are not ready to let agents make purchases.
The survey found that shoppers using AI agent referrals spend 8 percent more and are twice as likely to make a purchase.
Salesforce forecasts AI-driven recommendations will drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spending, representing a 13 percent increase from 2025.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- 20% of holiday shoppers worldwide are using AI agents for buying advice.
- 3 out of 4 shoppers trust recommendations from AI shopping agents.
- Traffic from AI tools to e-commerce sites has increased by 104% year-over-year.
Twenty percent of holiday shoppers are using AI agents as their first stop for research and advice, but they are not ready to have agents make purchases, according to the latest Salesforce research.
Also: What to know about early Black Friday sales

Salesforce surveyed more than 2,500 shoppers in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia and found that 74% of shoppers trust recommendations from AI agents. Salesforce research forecasts AI-driven shopping recommendations to drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spending, up 13% from 2025.
More from ZDNET

Brands are also being noticed by AI agents, with 30% of shoppers saying they were first introduced to a new brand via AI. And most importantly, 1 in 10 (11%) shoppers would avoid a brand if an AI agent told them to.
How retailers benefit from AI agents

Retailers that use AI shopping agents are seeing bigger orders and more loyal customers. The survey found that shoppers who use AI agent referrals are twice as likely to make a purchase. In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.
Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order. Brands that use AI agents are seeing seven times faster sales growth than brands without them.
Agents are advisors, not buyers (for now)
1 in 3 consumers has used an AI agent, including the widely adopted Meta Muse, now used by 12% of all consumers. Grok Bot is also in high demand.

The survey found that 28% of consumers give their agents multiple tasks per day. The most common use of AI agents is price comparisons, product reviews, and brainstorming for gift items. Brand discovery is a major benefit of AI agent use cases.

Agents as advisors are growing, but agents are not buying products yet, with only 19% of personal agent users using logic to check out. Only 9% of consumers allow their personal AI agents to have unrestricted access to their financial details, and 36% have set up a separate credit card for their AI agents.
Also: ZDNET’s favorite tech devices for 2026

The majority of consumers (73%) are not comfortable giving personal AI agents their payment information, and 49% are not interested in agents making purchases on their behalf. Consumers do not want to share their purchase history or personal data that could potentially lead to unwanted charges. Shoppers will abandon an AI agent after 2-3 mistakes. If an AI agent makes a bad recommendation, 1 in 3 consumers will blame the AI.
The future of shopping is more autonomous

Retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. The ability to detect intent, buying signals, sources of dissatisfaction, and other consumer-related buying patterns at machine scale (significantly faster and higher volume than human scale) will require retailers to invest in AI agentic engagement capabilities.

Today, AI agents advise consumers on their holiday shopping journeys, but in the very near future, they will autonomously make purchasing decisions with little to no involvement from their human counterparts. The future of shopping will be more autonomous, highly personalized, and nearly frictionless. Brands that invest in agentic AI will garner the most loyalty and future business.

articles.headline: It seems Robert Pattinson wasn’t the frontrunner to become James Bond, but Jeff Bezos, ‘heavily involved’ in the casting process, loved him
keyFacts: Amazon MGM selected Robert Pattinson as James Bond after Josh O Connor dropped out of the running.
According to Matthew Belloni, O Connor had reservations about the role and withdrew despite the gig being his to lose.
Jeff Bezos stated that he was heavily involved in the casting process and that everyone gravitated toward Pattinson during screen tests.
body: Robert Pattinson is James Bond: that much we already know. However, it seems the actor, despite his prowess and generational run, wasn’t Amazon’s first pick, not least because he is an established Hollywood superstar while Fleming’s masterpiece of a character usually gravitates toward lesser-known, up-and-coming actors.

But, apparently, Jeff Bezos was “heavily involved” in the casting choice, which ultimately saw Amazon MGM settling upon Pattinson. Prior to this decision, the role was meant to fall into the hands of Josh O’Connor, who’s been slowly garnering attention and fame through appearances in movies such as Challengers and, more recently, Disclosure Day .

According to Matthew Belloni ( via the Guardian ), O’Connor “had reservations about the baggage associated with the role from the start,” and eventually dropped out of the race, despite the fact that “the gig was his to lose.”

Pattinson was settled on after O’Connor dropped out of the race. Image via IMDb “He backed in and out of testing before deciding to do it – and soon afterward took himself out of the running,” Belloni, who correctly predicted Pattinson’s casting, said.
Choosing another candidate was thus absolutely necessary, and, according to Variety , Jeff Bezos involved himself “heavily” in the process.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance. It was immediately undebated. Denis, the director… we all gravitated toward Rob. Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he’s already so famous, like maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond,” Bezos himself told that outlet.

So I guess you could call it a combination of luck and Pattinson’s raw talent, which was irresistible even to Amazon’s chief. Pattinson is a once-in-a-generation talent , capable of pulling off a myriad of different characters and archetypes, and a person whose skills are never tied to highly-specific typecasting. I do find it a bit odd to consider him as Bond, but I’m positive he’ll knock it out of the park (so long as the script is good, and that, as we all know, is a very real plague of the Bond franchise).

articles.headline: Amid AI Industry Chaos, Microsoft and OpenAI Drop New Models for Coding and Work
keyFacts: Microsoft introduced seven new AI models at its Ignite conference, aiming to provide cheaper enterprise alternatives.
OpenAI released two new flagship model variants, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, which are now available globally to paying subscribers.
Nvidia experienced turmoil after its former CEO agreed to testify before Congress following revelations regarding his affairs.
body: It has been a wild week for AI, and it’s only Wednesday. Aside from outages, cheating scandals and upcoming IPOs, there are several new models available now. Microsoft dropped seven new versions of its MAI models at its Ignite conference, and OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, the next step forward for its flagship models.

First, Microsoft: At its Ignite developer conference on Tuesday, Microsoft introduced seven new AI models. They include MAI Cyber 2 Flash, MAI Code 2, MAI Image 2.7 and Dragon Copilot Transcribe — models meant to help with tasks in cybersecurity, coding, image generation and transcription.

It’s clear from Microsoft’s marketing that it is aiming to position its new tech as a cheaper alternative to OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s leading models, with many of these significantly cheaper to run at the enterprise level. That, plus its new licensed weight program, which lets companies customize the new AI models for their purposes, highlights how Microsoft is continuing to pitch its AI tech to the workplace.
More from CNET

Next, OpenAI: The ChatGPT maker dropped two new model variants of its flagship model, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra is the big model — it costs the most and uses the most firepower to handle complex tasks — and Sol is the “everyday” version. Both models beat their sibling models in OpenAI’s benchmarking. These are available to paying subscribers in ChatGPT and Codex globally now. (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)
The AI elephant in the room

While these new models might be useful for AI power users, they are far from most of the AI industry’s mind this week. During Tuesday’s earnings call, new interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress tried to assure investors that everything was “business as usual” after weeks of turmoil inside the company rocked the global economy. Nvidia cofounder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang’s multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, threw the company into chaos and have attracted the attention of the Securities and Exchange Commission and both chambers of Congress, where Huang has agreed to testify.

And let’s not forget about Anthropic, the Claude maker plans to become a public company this week, with the possible biggest-ever IPO slated for Thursday. Anthropic’s reportedly seeking an opening price of $78 per share, for a total valuation of $1.4 trillion — narrowly beating the other largest-ever IPO earlier this year, Elon’s Musk mega-conglomerate, SpaceX (including now SpaceXSI, because President Trump said so).

The Nvidia scandal caused a drastic 14% dip in its stock price during its first week and wiped out $1 trillion in the company’s value, but Anthropic investors don’t seem to be worried. At least, not publicly.

If nothing else, Anthropic’s IPO and the new models from OpenAI and Microsoft are stark reminders that the tech industry is nowhere near ready to slow down on AI. Even as financial, environmental and legal concerns mount — and arguably hit a fever pitch during the midterm elections — Big Tech is plowing ahead with generative AI.

articles.headline: The sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?
keyFacts: Cameron Bancroft and Usman Khawaja alleged that all Australian players and coaches knew about the 2018 sandpaper ball-tampering plot in South Africa.
Australia captain Pat Cummins strongly denied these claims, calling them utter nonsense and maintaining that he and the bowlers had no prior knowledge.
Former coach Darren Lehmann stated that he needs to process the new allegations before responding further.
body: - Published
The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.

Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.
Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.
However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.
Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.
Usman Khawaja
Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.
Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.
"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.
"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.
"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."
David Warner
Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.
The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.

After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.
In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."
He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".
"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.
"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"
Pat Cummins
The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.
Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.
In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".
"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."
Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."
Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.
Cameron Bancroft
Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.
He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.

In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".

Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa â the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".

He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.
In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.
"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.
"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."
Darren Lehmann
Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.
He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.
After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."
After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".
Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.
"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.
"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."
Steve Smith
Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.
After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.
He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.
Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.
Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.
"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."
Mitchell Marsh
Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.
Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.
"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.
"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."
Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.
Tim Paine
Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.
He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.

In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.
"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.
"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."
Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.
David Saker
Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.
Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.
Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.

In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.

"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chestâ¦ He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.
"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."
Mitchell Starc
Starc was an integral part of the vaunted Australia attack in Cape Town and remains so in the present day. He is ranked as the number one bowler in Test cricket by the International Cricket Council.

Left-armer Starc repeatedly denied knowledge of the sandpaper plot, including in the statement released with Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon in 2021, and in a news conference in the days after Khawaja's claims emerged.

Speaking on 10 November, Starc said: "Obviously, there's differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process at the time, and since, and I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed. My recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.
"I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then."
Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon

Along with Cummins and Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon have remained part of Australia's first-choice bowling unit in the eight years since the sandpaper scandal, forming one of the greatest four-man attacks in Test history.

Seamer Hazlewood and off-spinner Lyon joined Cummins and Starc in releasing a statement in 2021, responding to an interview given by Bancroft to the Guardian newspaper when he said the bowlers' involvement in the sandpaper plot was "self-explanatory".
Neither Hazlewood nor Lyon has spoken publicly since the fresh claims from Khawaja, Warner and Bancroft emerged.

Their statement released with Cummins and Starc in 2021 said: "We pride ourselves on our honesty. So it's been disappointing to see that our integrity has been questioned by some journalists and past players in recent days in regard to the Cape Town Test of 2018.
"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.
"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."
Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland
A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted â the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.
Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.

Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.
Speaking on 15 November, Sayers said: "I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used.
"It was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.
"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."
Spinner Holland, who retired in 2021, was also a back-up bowler on the trip.
He also said there was a meeting held in the fallout from Cape Town about players taking responsibility.
"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told newspaper The Australian.
"To Davey's [Warner's] credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it.
"To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."
Peter Handscomb
Batter Handscomb was Australia's 12th man on the day Bancroft was caught, making frequent trips between the field and the dressing room.
Bancroft's account alleges Handscomb was told by Lehmann, via walkie-talkie, to "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
Last week, following Khawaja's claims but before Bancroft spoke, Handscomb was asked for his recollections after making a century for Victoria in the Sheffield Shield against Western Australia.

On 11 November, Handscomb said: "I appreciate you have to ask these questions. I've had a nice day today, it's not really something that I want to comment on right now. I'll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing."
Graeme Hick
Former England batter Hick was part of the Australia backroom team on the South Africa tour of 2018.
Hick was made redundant by Cricket Australia as part of a series of cost-cutting measures in 2020.
Speaking to the Sydney Morning Herald last week, Hick said: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches, and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.
"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us'. To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.
"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.
"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."
The Sandpapergate Scandal
November 2026
Australian cricket was rocked by the sandpapergate scandal in 2018 and it is back in the headlines in 2026 following fresh allegations by former Australia batter Usman Khawaja.

articles.headline: Shelly’s new smart valve shuts off your home’s water before a leak becomes a flood

body: After releasing a $28 leak sensor earlier this year that conveniently runs off a battery for two years, Shelly is announcing an accompanying smart valve you can install on your home’s main water line to automatically turn off the flow when one of those sensors detects a problem. The Shelly Neo Smart Water Valve is available now through the company’s online store for $499.99, plus the cost of installation if you don’t trust your plumbing skills. It’s not a cheap solution, but it’s cheaper than the fallout of a leak turning into a disaster.
Shelly’s new smart valve shuts off your home’s water before a leak becomes a flood
The Neo Smart Water Valve works with Shelly’s sensors to stop a leak in about 12 seconds.

The Neo Smart Water Valve is designed to be installed on a standard US 1-inch thread connection (the company plans to launch additional size options next year) and is made from brass so it’s safe to use on plumbing carrying drinking water. It has an IPX7 waterproof rating so the valve will keep working if flooding means it ends up submerged. However, the valve lacks a battery of its own and requires a connection to a power source through an included USB adapter cable. Connecting it to a waterproof power bank instead of an outlet may be the best approach to ensure it still works during a power outage.

The smart valve connects to other devices over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth and is designed to integrate into existing smart home setups using webhooks, MQTT, or scripting for advanced users. In addition to shutting off the flow of water into your home in about 12 seconds, the valve also features an ultrasonic measurement system that tracks pressure, flow rate, your home’s consumption, and even the temperature of the water. Through the Shelly app, you can monitor all of that data in order to spot unusual usage patterns that could indicate a wasteful leak, or ensure the pressure doesn’t get high enough to damage pipes or appliances.

articles.headline: House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
keyFacts: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker after he won a closed-door caucus vote of 251-11.
Jeffries faces incoming Republican leader Jim Jordan in the upcoming House speaker race.
The official floor vote for speaker is scheduled to take place on January 3.
body: Jeffries won the closed-door caucus vote 251-11, leaving the Brooklyn Democrat one floor vote away from becoming the first-ever black speaker of the House.

The 56-year-old could have been nominated by acclamation, with no ballots cast and no count taken — an arrangement that would have kept his doubters off the record entirely. Jeffries changed course Tuesday, telling reporters he wanted to follow the approach Democrats took in 2018, the last time they won back the House.
Advertisement
On that occasion, Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) won her conference nomination with 203 members supporting her and more than 30 opposing her.
On Wednesday, Democrats were asked to give a “yes” or “no” answer to the question of whether they wanted Jeffries to lead the conference.

An online campaign to draft far-left Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) collected more than 150,000 signatures, but the “Squad” member never got in the race. At a Boston town hall this week, Pressley said she didn’t “need to be speaker of the House to speak for the people.”
Advertisement

Several incoming freshmen were cagey about their support going into the vote. Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy (D-NJ) predicted his colleagues would not “rubber-stamp” anything, while Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio), who flipped a GOP-held seat in the suburbs of central Ohio, said senior Democrats threatened to make his life “a living hell” if he didn’t support Jeffries.
Two incoming democratic socialists, Claire Valdez of New York and Melat Kiros of Colorado said they cared less about who leads the caucus than what their leaders plan to do.

Jeffries spent the days before the vote making his case to the lefties, announcing support for a higher federal minimum wage, a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and an expanded Medicare program.

The rest of the Democratic leadership nominees are Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) for majority leader, Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) for majority whip, Rep. Joe Neguse (D-Colo.) for assistant speaker and Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) for caucus chair.
Democrats are projected to hold at least 257 House seats next year, so Jeffries can afford to lose almost 40 of his own members and still reach the magic number of 218.
