The floor vote for speaker is scheduled for Jan. 3, with Jeffries and incoming Republican leader Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) the main combatants.

articles.headline: The US helped the world rein in nuclear weapons. Could it do the same for AI?
keyFacts: The unfinished work of nuclear governance offers an important lesson for those struggling with the risk of AI now: learning to live with a dangerous technology is not the same as eliminating its threat.
| Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto/Getty Images When Illinois Gov.

JB Pritzker talks about the threat of artificial intelligence, he offers an increasingly common point of comparison: it is a danger “on the level of nuclear weapons.” The comparison is not far-fetched.
body: The unfinished work of nuclear governance offers an important lesson for those struggling with the risk of AI now: learning to live with a dangerous technology is not the same as eliminating its threat. | Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto/Getty Images
When Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker talks about the threat of artificial intelligence, he offers an increasingly common point of comparison: it is a danger “on the level of nuclear weapons.”
The comparison is not far-fetched. If the international community found ways to constrain a potentially catastrophic technology once before, perhaps those arrangements can help us constrain another.

The trouble is that while nuclear nonproliferation may be a useful framework for thinking about regulating AI, it isn’t necessarily a good one. Not because the technologies are too different, but because nuclear nonproliferation hasn’t actually freed us from the prospect of nuclear war.

Nevertheless, the unfinished work of nuclear governance offers an important lesson for those struggling with the risk of AI now: learning to live with a dangerous technology is not the same as eliminating its threat.

What we might be able to do, however, is eliminate uncertainty about who’s building AI, what AI is capable of, and when AI puts people at risk. The US has done exactly that with nuclear weapons by declassifying information about the size and condition of its own arsenal, encouraging other nuclear powers to do the same.

Prioritizing transparency about AI wouldn’t eliminate the dangers altogether, but it might help us move forward more collectively as we strive to manage the very real risks of this emerging technology.
What the nuclear-AI analogy gets right… and wrong

Comparisons between AI and nuclear weapons have emerged not just from politicians and commentators but from those at the very top of the frontier AI food chain . For some AI leaders, nuclear weapons also represent an ideal model for oversight.

In a 2023 essay , OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, and Ilya Sutskever called for “something like an [International Atomic Energy Agency] (IAEA) for superintelligence efforts.” Their proposed international authority would “inspect systems, require audits, test for compliance with safety standards,” and restrict how the most powerful systems could be deployed.

The goal of such measures is to make the development of superintelligence safe, rather than prevent it, much as nonproliferation regimes stop short of banning nuclear weapons outright. Altman and his colleagues argue that the technology could deliver enormous benefits, while stopping its creation would be “unintuitively risky and difficult.”

Not everyone invoking nuclear governance draws the line in the same place. In September, AI researcher Yoshua Bengio told the UN Security Council that “frontier AI should be licensed like… medicine, aviation, and nuclear energy to incentivize safe development.” He also called for a universal constraint on AI development, one more expansive than those imposed on nuclear weapons: “No one, no company and no country, should develop an AI system that could cause large-scale harm.”

The real problem with such schemes may be figuring out how they would be enforced — and by whom. Sure, there are fewer states with nuclear weapons today than there could have been if nonproliferation had not become a policy priority for the US. However, this was not the result of diplomatic prowess or good-faith restraint. In the most important cases, it was a result of coercion by the US and its allies.

As Christopher David LaRoche and Ankit Panda, two nuclear experts at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, explained in Foreign Affairs: “South Korea and Taiwan gave up nascent weapons programs after intense pressure from the United States…and a threat to pull military support if they did not comply. Israeli airstrikes took out the Iraqi and Syrian programs; Libya surrendered its own under sustained U.S. and British pressure.”

In other words, unless the US seeks to go to war to prevent countries around the world from getting hands on frontier AI, nuclear nonproliferation is not the ideal mold for AI regulation. Plus, even in the face of a robust nonproliferation regime, a few states managed to slip through the cracks — India, Israel, North Korea, and Pakistan each acquired nuclear weapons.

Despite that, there are still fewer nuclear weapons in the world today than there were at the peak of the Cold War. But even the best-laid plans might not last forever. The arms control agreements that made such disarmament possible have all crumbled — whether due to cheating, repudiation, or expired treaties. Moreover, in addition to the increased number of states in possession of nuclear weapons, China has tripled its number of nuclear weapons just this decade.

These are the consequences of a regime built to manage a technology, rather than eliminate it. A similar frontier AI nonproliferation regime would govern who may build the most powerful systems, while leaving unaddressed the question of whether anyone should have that option in the first place.

The greatest lesson is for the US

Today, the threat of nuclear war persists. However, nuclear nonproliferation offers us one powerful takeaway: the United States, in particular, has a tremendous role to play in shaping the future of regulating frontier AI.

“In the nuclear domain specifically, the US historically has had a powerful norm-entrepreneurship function,” Panda told me. “What the United States does when it comes to nuclear weapons does get noticed by other countries and often gets adopted by other countries.”

This has historically involved leadership in transparency, Panda said. “The US, to its credit, is much more transparent than every other nuclear country when it comes to talking about things like command and control and what we do and don’t do.” For example, the US regularly declassifies and publishes data regarding the size of its nuclear weapons stockpile, fissile material inventories, and production facilities.

In a similar way, the US could lead the world in transparency about the frontier AI it is pursuing, the limits it might impose on that technology, and the safeguards in place to keep it under control.
This could take shape in a few ways, beginning with the US government’s own use of AI:

Before deploying a powerful and risky AI system, the government could disclose what risks it tested for, the conditions under which the system is considered reliable, its known limitations, and what findings would prevent deployment.

The US could explain which military decisions AI may contribute to and which require human authorization. This might, for example, involve distinguishing intelligence analysis from authority to initiate an attack. The government could also identify military applications of AI that it rules out altogether.
The US could publish accounts of failures or unexpected behavior, explaining whether a system was withdrawn, restricted, or retested after something went wrong.
These transparency measures should also extend to the private sector, and the government could require companies to:

Disclose dangerous-capability testing: This would involve requiring frontier developers to publish standardized summaries of tests for risks such as assisting cyberattacks, contributing to biological weapons development, or operating autonomously beyond intended limits.
Report serious incidents and near misses: Developers and deployers could be required to notify a regulator of significant safety failures, breaches, or unexpected dangerous behavior.

Publish the conditions for pausing development or withholding release: Companies could disclose in advance which findings would trigger additional safeguards, delay product launches, or halt further development.
As AI continues to reshape the world we live in, prioritizing transparency around the technology’s achievements — and limits — is one way to ensure that safety and security remain central.

articles.headline: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat. And, Nvidia won't reinstate Jensen Huang
keyFacts: Former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola defeated Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press.
Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones stated that the board does not intend to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang after his voluntary resignation.
The Pan American Health Organization announced that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status because a strain has persisted for over a year.
body: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat. And, Nvidia won't reinstate Jensen Huang
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories

Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press. Her victory gives Democrats 56 senators in the upcoming Congress. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for its general election, but Peltola secured a majority of first-place votes, eliminating the need for ranked-choice calculations. Her win flips a Senate seat in a state that President Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. The race's final days were tumultuous due to allegations that Peltola's team tried to recruit another candidate to the race to siphon votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied any involvement.

Trump has arrived in the Southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he is set to meet with China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday. This will mark the third time these two leaders have met this year. They are expected to discuss trade, investment and tariffs, which are currently on hold.

- 🎧 The meeting is about establishing a tone, as the U.S. and China have agreed to have constructive strategic stability, NPR's Jennifer Pak tells Up First. The two leaders will later be joined by Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting. The trio may discuss a peace deal for Russia's war in Ukraine, but China says that Europe must be included. Pak says China wants to show that a world leader won't make decisions without input from smaller countries. This is especially significant, Pak says, because these meetings take place on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC), where many smaller nations seek a voice in regional matters.

Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said in an earnings call yesterday that the board does not intend to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct," according to Jones. Huang acknowledged he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency. The board unanimously accepted his resignation. Earlier yesterday, Huang said he would return as CEO if the board permitted it and agreed to testify before Congress regarding national security issues surrounding the company.

- 🎧 NPR's John Ruwitch said that Jones clearly wanted to dispel rumors, and showed support for interim CEO Colette Kress. He said she "has been at the center of the company's extraordinary growth." Kress also participated in the call, maintaining a business-as-usual demeanor, Ruwitch says. Nvidia posted revenue exceeding $115 billion for the quarter, which isn't surprising, as the numbers were secured before Huang's recent departure. Tech analyst Gaurav Gupta from Gartner tells Ruwitch that any impact from new leadership won't be reflected in the numbers for several months. Jones said the board would try to decide on a permanent CEO as soon as possible without rushing the decision.

Major organizations have been experiencing widespread crashes of computer and online systems. Apple reported significant outages yesterday, and the U.S. National Security Agency also experienced a breakdown. As of this morning, no major disruptions seem to be occurring. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence that these incidents are related to one another or involve a malign actor or cybercriminal.

- 🎧 Cyber experts tell NPR's Greg Myre that artificial intelligence is uncovering previously undetected software flaws at an unprecedented pace. Companies are racing to patch or upgrade to address these vulnerabilities, but working under tight deadlines often leads to mistakes. As many systems undergo upgrades, people should anticipate disruptions along the way, Myre says. However, the optimistic perspective is that computer networks are expected to become more robust and resilient within the next year or two due to the improvements.
Deep dive

In recent years, highly concentrated products containing 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) have emerged online and at smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. These products, available as tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolates, contain one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom. Unlike kratom leaf products, 7-OH acts more like an opioid in the human brain. Some people use kratom to maintain long-term recovery from opioid addiction. Others say it helps them feel energized or focused. Users of 7-OH and kratom can show signs of addiction, and unclear product labeling makes it hard to determine the quantities consumed. Over the past decade, the U.S. government has tried to restrict these products, but public opposition has kept them legal. Recently, this situation has started to change.

- ➡️ In August, the Drug Enforcement Administration restricted the manufacture and sale of three semi-synthetic opioids from 7-OH and other related compounds. They were classified under the Controlled Substances Act alongside drugs like heroin and LSD.

- ➡️ Kratom advocates were concerned that new rules would impact products with "trace amounts" of the opioid MGPI. The American Kratom Association filed a federal lawsuit against the DEA on Aug. 26, seeking to keep natural kratom products with MGPI legal.

- ➡️ On Oct. 9, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a new recommendation on 7-OH and MGPI, leading the DEA to revise its stance to focus on restricting products with higher concentrations of these substances.
- ➡️ Opponents of the restriction argue that the products helped them avoid traditional opioids. Some point to the decrease in opioid deaths in the U.S.

- ➡️ The National Institute on Drug Abuse says that early studies indicate kratom and its compounds deserve more exploration as experimental treatments for substance use disorders, specifically opioid use disorder.
Real Talk With a Doc
Family physician Mara Gordon answers reader health questions monthly for NPR's special series Real Talk with a Doc. Send in your question to thrive@npr.org.

Artificial intelligence scribes help doctors take notes in various settings, from gynecologist visits to emergency rooms. Dr. Gordon says the technology saves time and allows her to focus entirely on her patients without the distraction of multitasking. But she also understands why patients might feel uneasy about new technology, and says she shares their concerns about privacy. Here's what Dr. Gordon says you should know about AI scribes:

- 🩺 The scribe uses "automatic speech recognition" technology to record the conversation between the doctor and the patient. After the visit, the recording is transcribed and turned into a medical note of the exam's findings and the doctor's decisions.

- 🩺 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) compliance is crucial for AI scribe services to ensure they protect patient privacy. Software companies must safeguard data by encrypting it, controlling access and implementing systems to prevent data breaches. Most companies delete recorded conversations after a specified period.

- 🩺 AI scribes can make mistakes, which is why doctors must review AI-generated notes before signing them and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software requires doctors to sign a user agreement, making them liable for all content in the medical record.
- 🩺Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates have raised concerns that this could widen health disparities.
- 🩺 You can always opt out of using an AI scribe during your doctor's visit. But opting out of AI in medicine more broadly could be tricky.

articles.headline: Xi greets Trump as he arrives in China, a rare move ahead of Putin talks
keyFacts: Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen on Wednesday ahead of upcoming talks.
The greeting reciprocates a similar gesture Trump made when Xi visited the White House in September, according to state-run media.
Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin are scheduled to hold an unprecedented trilateral meeting on Thursday during an Asia-Pacific summit.
body: SHENZHEN, China — In a rare and surprising move, Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of historic three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
It is believed to be the first time that Xi, in power for more than a decade, has been on hand to greet any foreign leader arriving in China.

He was reciprocating the personal greeting he had received from Trump in September, when the American leader met him at the plane upon his arrival for a White House state visit. Lawmakers from both parties had criticized Trump over the move, which is also rare for U.S. presidents.

A report by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, said that during Trump’s arrival in the city of Shenzhen on Wednesday, Xi noted the special trip the American president and first lady Melania Trump had made to welcome him at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.
“China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of returning goodwill with goodwill,” the Xinhua report said.

After Trump descended from Air Force One, a handshake between the two leaders turned into a quick hug as rows of military regiments and performers wearing bright pink and turquoise outfits stood at attention. A martial band played the American and Chinese national anthems as dancers waved flowers, pompoms and Chinese and American flags.

Xi’s gesture Wednesday most likely reflects a desire by him and his government to “show respect to Trump,” which they know he enjoys, William Yang, a senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, said in a post on X.
“It is likely also an attempt to uphold the positive rapport between Xi and Trump ahead of a potentially turbulent period in U.S.-China relations in the coming months,” he said.
When Trump last visited China in May, he was greeted at the airport in Beijing by Vice President Han Zheng.

Putin, who has a close relationship with Xi and has met with him 50 times as of Wednesday, did not receive a personal greeting from the Chinese leader when he arrived earlier at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport. Putin was instead met by Cai Qi, a close Xi adviser and member of the Politburo Standing Committee.
Xi has met with a number of world leaders, including Putin, as they gather in Shenzhen this week for a summit of Asia-Pacific economies.
Trump, Putin and Xi are holding an unprecedented trilateral meeting Thursday on the sidelines of the summit.

Ahead of his bilateral meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Putin said he expected “great potential benefits” from the trilateral talks, which have sparked anxiety in places such as Ukraine, Iran and the Beijing-claimed island of Taiwan, where officials worry the world’s three most powerful leaders could make decisions about their futures without consulting them.
In a briefing last week, a senior U.S. official said the trilateral meeting was unlikely to produce any sort of agreement, describing it as an “entry point” and “the first conversation.”

articles.headline: ‘He Needs To Be Removed’: CNN Medical Analyst Shreds RFK Jr. Over Measles Disaster
keyFacts: CNN medical analyst Dr. Jonathan Reiner demanded that President Donald Trump remove Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health and human services secretary.
The demand followed the United States losing its measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years.
Reiner blamed Kennedy's history of spreading vaccine misinformation for helping fuel the resurgence of the disease.
body: CNN medical analyst Dr. Jonathan Reiner on Tuesday demanded that President Donald Trump fire Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health and human services secretary after the United States lost its measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years.
“He needs to be removed,” said Reiner, a professor at George Washington University and longtime cardiologist to the late former Vice President Dick Cheney.

“The president should remove him,” he told CNN’s Kasie Hunt, joining a growing chorus of health experts blaming Kennedy’s history of spreading vaccine misinformation for helping fuel the resurgence of the disease.
Watch here:
“This is a historic failure of public health in the United States,” Reiner said, describing the previous elimination of measles in the country as “a triumph of 20th-century medicine.’”

“This is all brought on by this pernicious campaign in the last 20 years to cast doubt on the safety of a 60-year-old vaccine with almost complete efficacy … and a safety record tested in billions of people,” he argued.

“And there has been no greater purveyor of misinformation about this vaccine than America’s current health and human services secretary,” Reiner added. “RFK Jr. is the primary culprit in spreading doubt about this vaccine.”
